title: What is the smallest angle of symmetry with seven arms?
description: Seven equal radial arms share the full turn, so the smallest angle is three hundred sixty divided by seven. The division leaves a remainder, and the remainder is shared out as a fraction. Keeko's doubt is that an angle must be a whole number of degrees.
teaching_notes: One idea: when the arms do not divide the full turn exactly, the leftover is shared out as a fraction of a degree. Watch for students who round down to a whole number of degrees.

source: Consider a figure with radial arms having exactly 7 angles o
video_script.why: The child finds the smallest angle of symmetry for seven equal arms and writes the leftover as a fraction.
video_script.substitution: seven equal radial arms round a dot, the way the book draws radial arms
video_script.anchor: seven equal radial arms round a dot, drawn the way the book draws radial arms
video_script.wrong_answer: the gap is fifty one degrees
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko drops the remainder and says the gap is fifty one degrees.
video_script.payoff_line: The smallest angle is fifty one and three sevenths degrees

final_answer.spoken: three hundred sixty divided by seven is fifty one and three sevenths degrees, not a whole number

maths_rules: 7 equal arms share the full turn: smallest angle = 360 ÷ 7
7 x 51 = 357, and 360 - 357 = 3, so 360 ÷ 7 is 51 with remainder 3
the remainder 3 shared among 7 is 3/7, so the angle is 51 3/7 degrees
the remainder is not zero, so the angle is not a whole number
video_script.design: Seven equal arms round a dot. The full turn is shared by division, the remainder is shared out as sevenths, and the check puts the seven gaps back together to make the full turn. Keeko's doubt is that angles are whole numbers.
open_questions: The book's printed answer garbles the mixed fraction as 513/7; it is read as 51 3/7, which agrees with the division.

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step two, seven fifties are three hundred fifty, so try fifty one.
Seven times fifty one is three hundred fifty seven.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Three hundred sixty take away three hundred fifty seven leaves three degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Step three, share the leftover three degrees among the seven gaps.
<bookmark mark='frac'/>Each gap gets three sevenths of a degree.
Each gap is fifty one degrees and three sevenths of a degree.

beats.on_screen: check: 7 x 51 = 357, 7 x 3/7 = 3, 357 + 3 = 360; the remainder is not 0, so not a whole number

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step four, check by putting the seven gaps back together.
Seven times fifty one is three hundred fifty seven, and seven times three sevenths is three.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Three hundred fifty seven plus three is three hundred sixty, the full turn.
<bookmark mark='not'/>The remainder was not zero, so the angle is not a whole number.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The smallest angle is fifty one and three sevenths degrees.
It is not a whole number.
